name: Pilot, Measure, Scale
blurb: In a recent trial in Germany, 371 students in grades 7 through 9 used generative AI tools during six regular physics and English lessons. Some students got a tool designed to build motivation, some got a tool designed to teach learning strategies, and a comparison group used a plain chatbot.
title: Pilot, Measure, Scale
answer: In a recent trial in Germany, 371 students in grades 7 through 9 used generative AI tools during six regular physics and English lessons. Some students got a tool designed to build motivation, some got a tool designed to teach learning strategies, and a comparison group used a plain chatbot.

papers.why: Gives the book an evidence based frame for the draft then edit pattern: the teacher is both the trainer and the quality check on the tool, which is the human review gate stated as a research finding rather than a policy preference. The nine challenges are a ready made What can go wrong list for Chapters 17 and 20.
papers.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
papers.caveat: Covers 2000 to 2020, so entirely pre ChatGPT. Most included studies used AI to predict outcomes rather than to support live instruction. Only two of the studies involved pre service teachers.
papers.finding: Systematic review of 44 studies (2000 to 2020). AI helps teachers at three points: planning (identifying student needs), implementation (immediate feedback and timely intervention during activities), and assessment (automated scoring). Teachers also serve as the models AI is trained on and as the checkers of AI scoring accuracy. Nine challenges recur: limited algorithm reliability, limited technical capacity (weak on graphics and figures), thin school infrastructure, systems that do not transfer across settings or languages, weak validity in assessment, low teacher technical knowledge, low teacher interest, slow feedback, and feedback that is not adaptive.

papers.why: Trust, not capability, decides adoption. The two explanation types are a concrete design for any AI PD session in Chapter 20 and for the teacher accuracy check in Chapter 17.
papers.title: Teachers' trust in AI ‐powered educational technology and a professional development program to improve it
papers.caveat: Abstract only. Science teachers and one grading tool; sample size not stated in the abstract.
papers.finding: Experiments with K12 science teachers using an AI grading tool on synthetic and real data. Two explanations reduced teacher concern and raised trust: how the AI makes decisions compared with human experts, and how it complements rather than replaces the teacher. Presents a professional development program and discourse analysis of teachers who completed it.

papers.why: Ease of use beat usefulness. For Chapter 20, this argues for picking simple tools first and for coaching that connects AI to active learning pedagogy.
papers.title: Influence of Pedagogical Beliefs and Perceived Trust on Teachers’ Acceptance of Educational Artificial Intelligence Tools
papers.venue: International Journal of Human Computer Interaction (Taylor and Francis)
papers.caveat: Abstract only, closed access. Self reported acceptance, not observed use. Korean context.
papers.finding: Survey of 215 teachers in South Korea, structural equation model extending the technology acceptance model. Teachers with constructivist beliefs adopt educational AI tools more than teachers with transmissive beliefs. Perceived usefulness, ease of use, and trust all matter, and ease of use was the strongest predictor of acceptance.

papers.why: Same mechanism as paper 47: use drives acceptance. Supports low stakes hands on exposure as the first PD step.
papers.title: Generative AI and Teachers’ Perspectives on Its Implementation in Education
papers.caveat: Abstract only, no open license. Perceptions; the authors note views may not translate into action.
papers.finding: Survey of 147 teachers on generative AI. Teachers were positive regardless of teaching style; the more often they used GAI, the more positive they became. Teachers believed GAI could support their own PD and be valuable for students.

papers.why: Matches paper 38 and 41: teachers trust AI for planning before grading. Chapter 17 should sequence adoption that way.
papers.title: An investigation of teachers' perceptions of using ChatGPT as a supporting tool for teaching and learning in the digital era
papers.caveat: Abstract only, no open license. 40 teachers, private schools, UAE.
papers.finding: Mixed methods with 40 middle and high school teachers in Dubai and Abu Dhabi private schools. Teachers see the most benefit from ChatGPT in lesson planning and teaching activities and less in assessment and feedback. Biggest challenges: bias and accuracy of information and lack of human interaction.

papers.why: Gives districts a ready survey to measure staff trust before and after PD, turning adoption readiness into a number. Shows the blocker is not fear of job loss but the sense that AI cannot see the whole child.
papers.title: An Instrument for Measuring Teachers’ Trust in AI-Based Educational Technology
papers.caveat: Single country, science teachers only, 87% female, exploratory factor analysis only (no CFA yet). Scenario was a clustering tool, not generative AI.
papers.finding: Validated a 24-item teacher trust instrument (132 Israeli high-school science teachers, EFA, 7-factor model fit well). Eight dimensions: perceived benefits, lack of human characteristics, lack of transparency, anxieties, self-efficacy, required shift in pedagogy, preferred means to increase trust, AI vs human advice. Teachers rated benefits high (mean 3.8/5) and self-efficacy high (3.8), but trust AI advice less than a peer or expert (2.7). Fear of replacement was low (2.8). Knowing how the tool decides would raise trust (3.7). Lack of human traits (emotion, student history, intuition) was the top reason for distrust (3.5).

papers.why: Principal practices for rolling out AI policy.
papers.title: School principals' technology and transformational leadership practices for spreading the adoption of an artificial intelligence in education (AIED) policy
papers.finding: 16 Israeli principals spreading a national AI policy used technology leadership (PD, shared leadership, parent and partner links) and transformational leadership.

papers.title: Approaches to Artificial Intelligence Policy Development in K–12 School Districts
papers.finding: Interviews with six Colorado district leaders: early AI policy relied on informal guidelines, student bans, or updated acceptable use policies; gaps in PD and evaluation.

papers.title: Leveraging complex systems: Leading for transformative change
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Leading transformative change with AI through a complex systems lens.

papers.title: Towards responsible AI in education: A Delphi-AHP-based framework for evaluating educational large language models
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 10
papers.finding: Delphi-AHP framework for evaluating educational LLMs responsibly.

papers.title: Leading the AI transformation in schools: it starts with a digital mindset
papers.finding: German school leaders: digital mindset (agility, empathy) and ambidextrous leadership predicted AI implementation.

papers.why: Names the chicken-and-egg stall many US districts face and gives the three-direction frame for the book's structure. Recommends collective will over a lone principal or champion teacher.
papers.title: An investigation of barriers to Hong Kong K-12 schools incorporating Artificial Intelligence in education
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.finding: Case study of two Hong Kong K-12 schools, 10 stakeholder interviews. Frames AIED as three directions: learning from AI, learning about AI, learning with AI. Found both external barriers (no official curriculum guideline, limited PD, resources) and internal barriers (disputed views of what AI education is, teachers treating coding and STEM as the destination). Barriers are linked, so fixing high-linkage barriers eases others. Schools wait for government guidance while government waits for school exemplars.

papers.why: Confirms Nazaretsky: teachers trust human advice more. New teachers will not fix this by themselves; training on what models are and when they help is needed.
papers.title: Algorithm appreciation or aversion? Comparing in-service and pre-service teachers' acceptance of computerized expert models
papers.venue: Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, vol 2
papers.caveat: Swiss sample, judgment tasks not classroom tools, pre-generative AI.
papers.finding: Behavioral and survey study. In-service and pre-service teachers both preferred advice from a human school counselor over an expert model, to a similar degree, so younger teachers are not less algorithm averse. Acceptance depended on task difficulty. In-service teachers lacked knowledge of expert models but thought models could beat humans on some tasks.

children.name: The Five Phases
children.blurb: The Five Phases is a staged method for adopting AI in a school: assess readiness, choose the pilot, set up governance, run and evaluate, and scale what works.

children.name: Phase One: Assess Readiness
children.blurb: Phase One: Assess Readiness is the first step in piloting AI in a school or district, where leaders check whether people, policies and support systems are actually ready before tools are rolled out.

children.name: Phase Two: Choose the Pilot
children.blurb: Phase Two of a school AI rollout means choosing a first pilot that begins with a clearly defined problem rather than a product, and keeping that pilot low in risk and high in visibility.

children.name: Phase Three: Set Up Governance
children.blurb: Phase Three of a pilot means completing governance before any student touches the tool: the tool is placed on the approved list with its limits recorded, a data privacy agreement is signed when student information is involved, a named owner is accountable for results, and families receive a short plain notice.

children.name: Phase Four: The Six Week Pilot
children.blurb: The Six Week Pilot is the fourth phase of a school's adoption process, in which two or three volunteer teachers use a tool as designed for six weeks while tracking one main measure recorded before and after.

children.name: What to Measure
children.blurb: The most common AI pilot measures, such as logins, minutes of use and prompt counts, only show that a tool was opened, not that anything improved.

children.name: Reading the Results Honestly
children.blurb: Reading pilot results honestly means treating the numbers with care before deciding to scale a tool.

children.name: How to Say No
children.blurb: Exit criteria are the conditions agreed before a pilot begins that tell a school when to stop using a tool.

children.name: The One Page Pilot Record
children.blurb: The One Page Pilot Record is a single, two-minute-readable summary that captures what a pilot tested, how it was measured, what happened, and what was decided.

children.name: Phase Five: Scale What Works
children.blurb: Phase Five of the pilot process is about scaling a tool that has already passed its first test, but doing so gradually rather than all at once.

children.name: Pilots Outside the Classroom
children.blurb: Pilots outside the classroom apply the same pilot, measure, scale discipline to operational tools such as routing software or translation tools, even though those tools never enter a classroom.

sections.body: This section is about how a school tries an AI idea without committing the whole year or budget to it, moving from first interest to districtwide use through a staged method. The book describes a five phase approach that covers the readiness check, vendor evaluation, the governance steps from Chapter 3, a six week pilot, and the decision to scale or stop. It notes that the same method applies whether the tool is a lesson planner, a tutor, or a bus routing system. The book grounds this in a German trial where 371 students in grades 7 through 9 used generative AI tools across six regular physics and English lessons, with some getting a motivation tool, some a learning strategies tool, and a comparison group a plain chatbot. On effort, knowledge, and use of learning strategies, neither designed tool beat the plain chatbot.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The book finds that careful design by experts can still produce no clear gain in real classrooms, so a product chosen from a conference booth deserves at least the same scrutiny. What works is testing before scaling, with a small group, a clear measure, a starting point, and a date to decide, and a pilot record of one page per tool holding the problem statement, measure, baseline, result, and decision. What does not work is the pilot that cannot fail, where a tool is chosen, a launch is planned, no baseline is recorded, no exit criteria are set, and the rollout goes ahead anyway, leaving the district paying for a tool nobody can show made a difference. A vendor's case study is not evidence, and neither is a survey of teachers who liked the tool, while a before and after measure with a comparison where possible is what counts. The rule the book holds to is that a pilot is not a soft launch that builds momentum for a decision already made, it is a fair test allowed to fail, and a pilot that ends with a clear no is a success.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move through the method in order, so a leader would start with The Five Phases for the overall shape and then work through Phase One: Assess Readiness, Phase Two: Choose the Pilot, and Phase Three: Set Up Governance before running Phase Four: The Six Week Pilot. A teacher or leader setting up the test would go to What to Measure for the table of measures that show real results and to Reading the Results Honestly for how to interpret them, then to How to Say No for the exit criteria that make refusal easier, with The One Page Pilot Record capturing the whole thing on a single page per tool. Phase Five: Scale What Works covers the decision to expand, and Pilots Outside the Classroom extends the same method to tools beyond teaching, such as a bus routing system. A parent or board member would go to The One Page Pilot Record and the board question about what each paid tool measured, what it found, and who decided to scale it, since in many districts the honest answer is that there was no pilot, only a purchase.
